items.passage: Manila came past the compartment window in strips of laundry and rain. Father Kiet had brought the old hymnal from Arisa's childhood parish, and he opened it on his knee to the third hymn, where someone long ago had penciled a softer word beside the printed Tagalog, a word that turned the line from an order into a request. Arisa said her grandmother had sung it that way every Sunday, loudly enough that the pews around her sang it too. She had not been inside a church, she added, in eleven years. Kiet said the bishop preferred the printed word. At the next station he mentioned that the new hymnals would be printed without margins. Arisa said nothing. She took the book, found the same word on two later pages, faint, in the same hand, and traced each one until the graphite shone, never pressing hard enough to smudge it. When the train slowed for her stop, she borrowed the pencil from his pocket, sharpened it against the window latch, and gave it back to him point first.

items.passage: What does a prize weigh in a language you have only half learned? She repeated her speech; she knew nothing else by heart. Wira kept at his cutting table, laying flat blue chalk lines across the wool. Before each coat left the shop he brushed the lines away, and a customer who once asked to keep the pattern was told that a coat should not carry its measurements around. Zihan noticed he no longer corrected her in front of anyone. On the mornings after the cousins visited, a few words appeared at the edge of the table, faint, in that same blue, gone by noon. She began arriving early. In February a cousin asked her to recite again, and she answered instead in a sentence she had built herself, clumsy and new. Wira, sweeping chalk dust into his palm, did not look up, though he stopped sweeping.

items.passage: Still borrowing my shuttle, Imtiaz? Lucien asked from the doorway, the rent book under his arm. She did not stop the loom. For eleven years she had rented the corner room of the Lyon cooperative from him, and for nine the walnut shuttle he had lent her, the winter her own cracked, had crossed her warp thousands of times a day. A new shuttle, bought that spring, still lay in its paper in a drawer. Lucien picked it up, weighed it, and set it down. He walked to the shelf where her finished bolts were stacked and ran his thumb along an edge; every length carried the same faint ridge, a catch in the weave that no other loom in the building made. Buyers now asked for it by name. He said, mostly to the window, that the shuttle had learned her hand better than it had ever learned his. Imtiaz offered to return it after the current order. Lucien wrote a figure in the rent book, crossed it out, wrote a smaller one, and asked whether the spring wool had arrived.

items.passage: Gyms remember everything. Jianguo spun a basketball on one finger. Caoimhe asked whether the janitor's watch had been checked against the bell, whether the hasp had been loose before, who else held keys. Each question came out clipped and orderly, and she wrote the answers in her diary as though preparing for a hearing. Then the deputy turned a page. A first-year's mother had phoned: Jianguo had sat with her son in the library until half four, going over fractions. The ball slowed and dropped into his lap. Caoimhe closed the diary. She tried to remember whether he had ever told her about the library, and could not, and found that the question she wanted to ask now was not one for the deputy. She set her hand on the bench, near his, and left it there.

Behind the dishcloths lay a child's school report, the pupil's surname the old owner's, the address this house, the dates the missing winters. Then the June storm came through the back wall, and while I pulled swollen boards from the water I lifted a loose slat and found a box she had left there: twelve blank journals, hand-sewn, one for each month she would be gone, the first marked with my name, Ximena, and the week she left. I read the date several times. I thought of my last message, a joke about a man who wanted his dog's diary bound in calfskin, and could not remember what I had been avoiding by sending it. The carpets were sold, the books gone to the mosque library; only the brass samovar remained, and each of us had politely offered it to the other. __I had always assumed she kept it because it was too heavy to give away.__ The letters, written to her sister across thirty years, mention it often but only in passing: polished for Nowruz, dented on the stairs in Shiraz, mended by a man who overcharged. Bahram read out a line from a letter dated the spring after our father died: she had set the samovar going before she unpacked a single plate, so the new rooms would hear something familiar. He read it again, more slowly. We sat until the gatekeeper began locking the side entrance. Then Bahram folded the letter and said he would bring the car around; if we laid the samovar on a blanket, it would fit in the back.

items.passage: Mabel had driven the harbor route for nineteen years and regarded the 7:40 as hers in roughly the way a cat regards a windowsill. Nikhil boarded it each morning at the chapel stop with a flask and a folded crossword, and if he was late she waited, engine running, and told the other passengers it was the timetable. On Monday the chapel stop was gone. The council had moved it two hundred yards on, to a glass shelter by the fish market, having consulted no one and least of all Mabel. Nikhil was waiting there and apologized when she drew up, as if he had signed the order himself. Mabel informed him that it was all the same to her where people chose to stand. Three rules hung by the guesthouse door:
no shoes past the mat, no lamps past ten,
no questions for the brothers while they pray.
I kept them, and a fourth I never wrote,
which was my daughter's name, Leila, unsaid.
My grandson broke it on the second night,
up on one elbow in the narrow bed:
why does my mother never come with us?
And I, Soraya, gave him Samarkand,
the blue of the domes, the tiles, the thousand stars
the masons pressed by hand into the vaults.
He heard me out, the way a child will,
then asked again, more quietly, the same.
I tell it now the way I'd tell a sum
I added wrong for years and still recite,
each star a coin laid down against a fare
too large for coins. That night I broke a rule.
The lamp stayed lit past ten. He asked once more.

Lingering frustration with the boy for pressing a question she avoided

The following week I found him in the reading room of the district library in Shanghai, where the radiators ticked and nobody spoke above a breath. He had a calculus textbook open and, beside it, a ledger ruled in two columns, the kind his father kept at the noodle shop on Wuding Road. Without looking up he said his father's hands shook too much now for the evening shift. I had come with a few sentences about commitment. I sat down instead and asked which column was rent. He turned the ledger toward me. I checked his sums; he checked mine; neither of us mentioned basketball. My name is Tane, and I am not a sentimental coach. The rule is still on the gym wall, unchanged. Practice, these days, is on Tuesdays and Thursdays, the evenings the shop closes at six.
